I've farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. At 64, I know exactly what this soil and climate will give me if I work it right. The North China Plain double-crop rotation — winter wheat then summer maize on the same plots — is what I've always done, and there's no reason to change it. The markets are reliable, and my 12 mu of dryland-capable irrigated fields are suited for nothing else as profitable.

My concern this year, as always, is water. The water table here has been dropping my entire adult life. I'll irrigate wheat three times — seeding moisture to get good germination, jointing water for stem extension, and one more at grain filling. I won't do the overwintering irrigation many neighbors still do; I've learned over the years it's often wasteful if autumn rains were decent. For maize, the summer rains usually carry it, but I'll pump twice to be safe.

I'm educated enough to know that applying all the nitrogen at once is wasteful and causes lodging. I split it — base fertilizer before planting, topdress at jointing for wheat, and a mid-season topdress for maize. I use the 济麦22 wheat variety; it yields well and has good disease resistance. For maize I use 郑单958 — proven hybrid, I've used it for years.

I'll hire the village machinery cooperative to deep plough before wheat planting in October. After wheat harvest in June I'll direct-seed the maize with minimal disturbance — saves soil moisture and cuts labor, which matters at my age.
